item.title: Why Video Compresses 100×: Redundancy, YUV, I/P/B Frames and GOP
item.description:
The later posts on browser codec selection and the streaming protocol panorama keep leaning on H.264, I-frames and GOP — this post fills in the foundation first: what actually happens when a stream of pixels turns into a few Mbps. No math derivations — mechanisms, each tied to its engineering consequence (latency, seeking, corruption, storage).

Start with some arithmetic.

How big is uncompressed video

One 1080p (1920×1080), 30fps, 8bit RGB stream:

text
1
2
3
4

pixels per frame = 1920 × 1080 = 2,073,600
bytes per frame = 2,073,600 × 3 (RGB) ≈ 5.93 MB
per second = 5.93 MB × 30 ≈ 178 MB/s
bitrate ≈ 1.49 Gbps

That is 10.7 GB per minute. 4K (3840×2160) multiplies by another 4: ~42.7 GB/min. Sixteen surveillance cameras recording for a month at these rates is beyond any storage system. In practice 1080p surveillance streams run 2–8 Mbps — a compression ratio on the order of several hundred to one. Compression is not an optimization; it is the precondition for video existing at all.

item.title: Inside H.264: the Encode Pipeline and the Bitstream, from Residuals and Quantization to NALU and SPS/PPS
item.description: The previous post covered the frame level: I/P/B, GOP, PTS/DTS. This one goes inside H.264 to answer two questions: what pipeline turns a frame into bytes, and what SPS/PPS/NALU each do in the bitstream. H.264 is not the newest — H.265 and AV1 both compress better (selection guide) — but it has the largest installed base, dominates surveillance/GB28181 links, and every later standard evolved from its skeleton. Once you take it apart, the differences in H.265/H.266/AV1 read easily.

item.title: H.264 / H.265 / H.266 Web Frontend Playback: Which Generation to Pick in 2026
item.description: The previous post traced bitstream structures from H.265 through AV1/AVS; this one comes back to the browser: which generation should you actually use. In the MiBee NVR surveillance-dashboard project, should the frontend pull H.264 or H.265 from all 16 cameras? A seemingly simple question that gets deeper the more you dig. H.265 needs only half the bitrate of H.264 at the same quality, saving both bandwidth and storage. But plenty of online sources still claim “H.265 browser support is poor, Firefox doesn’t support it, you need to install extensions.” Which of these claims still hold?
